D:\\wt\\lcfdump\\vlog\\lcfdump\\voz\\b00.text: That can is tipping over one little chicken breast, honey, and you're going to think I've lost my mind. Most of us figure a supper needs a knife and an hour at the stove. It doesn't. It's mid -October in Iowa, the first cold nights, the furnace running, and a lot of you are eating supper alone. You all asked for more, 10 new ones. Not one of them needs a knife. What goes in this little dish and the lid on top that nobody has to roll out? I'm saving for number 10, so stay with me. Do you think a supper for one has to be sad, honey? I'm Loretta, 81, from Story County, Iowa. Harold and I had 51 years, and he's been gone nine. I cook for one in my farmhouse now. After the first video, so many of you living alone wrote in that I went back to my little book for 10 more. The church ladies have a salmon trick, and that's number three.

Number nine gets you a baked potato without all that waiting. And first, a meatloaf with no loaf pan. Number one is the supper you'd never think to make for one. Meatloaf, honey? You picture a loaf pan, a big bowl, and a whole evening at the counter. Mine is a meatloaf the size of a fist, done in 30 minutes in the toaster oven. Half a pound of ground beef, two tablespoons of beaten egg, three of breadcrumbs, two of milk, two of chopped onion, and two of ketchup, mixed gently with your hands. Pat one little loaf onto the lined pan just the way it's written on page 121. Spread a spoon of ketchup on top. Toast your oven at 350 and let it rest five minutes before you slice. Here it sits, one slice on one plate at a table set for one. Ground beef needs to reach 160 degrees in the middle, so check it.

It makes two plates, and that second slice is tomorrow's cold sandwich with mustard, the best one you'll eat all week. Danny films every one of these for me, honey, and he's the one who reads me the comments. He sat right here at my kitchen table and read them to me, one after another, and you all kept asking for more. I had to take my glasses off and wipe them. A woman needs a minute sometimes. Those comments are why I went back to my little book. Have you ever stood at your stove at supper time and not wanted to cook for one? I know that feeling, honey. So every one of these 10 is one page of my little book, Supper for One. The link is in the description below, and it holds all 140 small suppers. The church lady's salmon trick is still coming at number three. Right here on this channel is the first one, honey.

It's called 10 Dump and Bake Suppers for seniors living alone, no chopping, no stirring. If you missed it, go take a look. None of its suppers come back here. Let's move on to number two, the chicken thigh that started the toaster oven chapter of my book. Number two is on page 120 where the toaster oven chapter began. One of you wrote to me that all she has is a little toaster oven. That stopped me cold honey. Why heat a big oven for one chicken thigh? I wrote that right in my book. So heat the toaster oven to 400 degrees and line the small pan. Toss four baby potatoes halved with half the oil and a little salt and set them around the edge. Rub one bone and thigh with the rest of the oil, a crushed garlic clove, oregano, salt and pepper and lay its skin up in the middle. Bake 35 minutes then squeeze half a lemon over it all.

Turn the potatoes once, halfway through, because toaster ovens heat more from the top. Cook the chicken to 165 degrees next to the bone. One plate, crisp skin and potatoes all around it. That little oven has been good company to me, honey. Some nights the kitchen gets so quiet, you can hear the furnace kick on. The first supper I baked in that little toaster oven after Harold passed, I set one plate at the table, just one, and I sat down to it. I didn't rush through it, honey. It was a small plate, but it was a start. Now, number three, the church lady's salmon. Number three, page 124. The church ladies made me promise to tell you this one. Folks figure a salmon filet dries out to nothing in a little oven. A spoon of mayonnaise keeps the salmon moist. That's the lady's trick, right there on the page. Mayonnaise is just oil and egg.

It browns and seals in the juice. Spread that spoon on with a little mustard, sprinkle the crumbs on top, and cook it to 145 degrees. It's the most I spend on any of the 10, and it makes one plate. Look at that golden top and the fish coming apart on your fork. On a cold night, honey, that's worth every bit of it. The baked potato shortcut for when you can't wait an hour is still coming at number nine. For now, number four is a sweet potato, and it's waiting on you. Number four is a meatless night, built from a can of beans and a jar of salsa. Most folks reach for a can of soup and call it supper. Page 126 calls this one a meatless supper with plenty of body, and it is. Put foil under the sweet potato, honey, because it drips sugar that burns on the bottom of the toaster oven.

Bake one pricked sweet potato at 400 degrees for 45 minutes until it's soft. Split it, mash the inside a little with a fork, and fill it with a third of a cup of rinsed black beans and two tablespoons of salsa. Top it with two tablespoons of shredded cheese and bake five minutes more until it melts. Then add a spoon of sour cream. Picture that cheese going stringy over the beans. It makes one plate. Next is number five, the Friday Supper of Every Church in Iowa. Number five is the fish supper we ate every Friday on page 131. Most homes grab a box of fish sticks and call it done. Mine is one cod or haddock fillet on a greased pan, salted lightly. Mix two tablespoons of crushed crackers, a tablespoon of melted butter, a pinch of paprika and dried parsley, and press it on top.

Heat the oven to 400 degrees and bake 12 to 15 minutes until it flakes. Squeeze lemon over it. It costs about $2 .20 and it makes one plate. A little oven sits the food close to the coils so those crumbs can brown before the fish is ready. When they do, I lay a loose piece of foil over the top, my tip from page 119. Feel the flakes give way under your fork. Next, the fall supper of the season, a pork chop on apples. Number six, page 123 is the fall supper. Most homes fry a chop hard in a skillet and the grease spits all over the stove top. Mine goes in the little pan with half an apple, sliced thin. I toss the slices with melted butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, then lay them on the lined pan. Season one boneless chop, three quarters of an inch thick and set it right on top.

Heat the toaster oven to 375 degrees and bake 20 to 25 minutes. The page says pork is done at 145 degrees, then rest at 3 minutes. Don't skip that rest honey, it makes one plate about $2 .20. The whole kitchen smells like fall. Lift the chop onto the plate and spoon the apples over it. Now for something lighter, a crisp little pizza. Number 7, page 125. This is the lightest supper of the 10. Most folks slap the sauce right onto a soft tortilla, pile on the cheese and push it in the oven. Then the middle goes limp and soggy. My little trick is simple. Crisping the tortilla first keeps it from going soggy under the sauce. So I heat the toaster oven to 400 degrees and bake the plain tortilla alone until it starts to crisp.

Only then do I spread two tablespoons of sauce, a third of a cup of mozzarella, and a few slices of pepperoni or leftover vegetables. Back in it goes until the whole top is bubbling. It makes one pizza and I slide it onto one plate at a table set for one. The edge snaps when you bite it, honey, and that's the whole point. Now, about that little square on your screen, are you eating supper by yourself tonight? If you'd like all 10 on paper, plus the rest of the 140, point your phone at the little square on the screen. It takes you straight to my little book, Supper for One, one page for every supper. And that little dish you saw me pour the can into, it's still waiting for you at number 10. Next is the Toasted Ham and Swiss. Number eight, page 128, is the Toasted Ham and Swiss.

D:\\wt\\lcfdump\\vlog\\lcfdump\\voz\\b01.text: Most homes make a cold sandwich at the counter, eaten standing up with the plate still in the sink. Mine gets toasted and it comes off the rack hot. Butter the outside of two slices of bread, then build the sandwich with two slices of ham and one slice of Swiss cheese. Set it on a small piece of foil because cheese that drips on the coils smokes the whole house. Toasted in the toaster oven at 400 degrees, four minutes aside. Meanwhile, warm a bag of frozen soup in a pot. Set the sandwich on one plate with a cup of soup beside it at a table set for one. It makes one sandwich and takes 10 minutes. Soft, warm, and ready in your hands, honey. Bernice told me once, down in the basement kitchen at Zion United Methodist, Loretta, a supper doesn't need a knife to be a supper. For years I thought it had to sit on a plate with a knife beside it.

She was right, and that toasted sandwich proves it. I promised you a baked potato for people who can't wait the whole hour. Number nine is that shortcut, and it's coming right up. Number nine, page 122. Most homes figure a baked potato means the big oven roaring for an hour. My book puts it this way. One potato, an hour, and no electricity bill like the big oven. So mine goes in the toaster oven, heated to 400 degrees. Scrub it, prick it six times with a fork, and rub it with oil and salt. Set it right on the rack and bake it 50 to 60 minutes until a knife slides in. Short on time, microwave it five minutes first, then 15 in the toaster oven to crisp the skin. Split it open, add a pat of butter, and set it on one plate at a table set for one. Sour cream or cheese if you like. That whole plate is the cheapest supper of the 10, honey.

Now, remember that little dish from the very start? Number 10. Number 10, page 127. The little dish from the very first shot. Most homes reach for a pie plate and a rolling pin, then fuss over a crust. Here you stir a half cup of cooked chicken, a half cup of frozen mixed vegetables, a third of a cup of cream of chicken soup, and two tablespoons of milk right in a little baking dish. Then comes the lid nobody has to roll out. Two triangles of refrigerated crescent dough laid over the top. Bake it in the toaster oven for 20 to 22 minutes until golden and bubbling. Spoon it onto your good plate at a table set for one. Freeze the rest of the crescent dough raw, two triangles to a bag, and freeze the rest of the soup in portions so the next one is ready to go. On a cold night with the furnace running, honey, that's a real supper.

Let's look back at all 10. Let's walk back through them. Number 1. The little meatloaf on a pan. Number 2. The lemon and garlic chicken thigh. Number 3. The church lady salmon. Number 4. The stuffed sweet potato. Number 5. The baked cod with crumb topping. Number 6. The pork chop on apple slices. Number 7. The tortilla pizza. Number 8. The hot ham and cheese. Number 9. The baked potato in the toaster oven. Number 10. The little pot pie under its crescent lid. Pick the one for tonight. All 10 are pages in one little book. Open the drawer by your stove, the one full of takeout menus. My little book, Supper for One, has 140 small suppers for seniors living alone, one page each. Next to every one is what it cost me at my grocery store this fall and my little trick for it. The link is in the description below.

Tonight, slide one menu back and find your page instead. Your homework for tonight is a small one, honey. Pick one of the 10, just one. Then set the table for one. Use the good plate. You're worth it, the way I wrote it in my book. When you've eaten, tell me which number you picked. Tell me which number you're making first this week, honey. And what are you putting in your baked potato? Butter, cheese, or something you'd never admit to? Danny and I read every comment at the kitchen table. And if pot roast is more your speed, I've got something for you. If you still cook a pot roast on Sundays, you'll want my other channel. It's called Loretta's Church Kitchen. There's a video there called Most People Are Cooking Pot Roast Wrong. Try these church lady tricks for fork tender roast. I won't give you any of those tricks here, honey. Go on over and watch it some cold October evening.

Then come back here next week. Next week I've got more small suppers for one for you, honey. So keep your can opener right where you can reach it and I'll see you then. Cooking for one isn't sad. Eating crackers over the sink is sad. So set a place for yourself, light a candle, use the good plate and call somebody while you eat. I'm so glad you stayed with me tonight. May the Lord bless your little table on this cold October night. Goodbye for now, honey, and God bless you.
